media:group.media:title: Can a heart heal itself?
media:group.media:description:
After a heart attack, up to one billion heart cells can be lost.
Unlike most cells in our body, heart cells can’t fix themselves when damaged.
This reduces the strength of the heart and can lead to heart failure and ultimately death.
Now scientists have developed a treatment that ‘reawakens’ heart muscle cells so they start to divide, and help repair damaged muscle following a heart attack.
It has shown promising results in animal trials, and the next step is to refine it and test its safety and effectiveness in humans.
This is an exciting step towards a potential curative treatment for heart disease, which could improve the quality of life of millions of people around the world.
Find out more here 👉 https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/treatment-promotes-repair-after-heart-attack

entry.title: Can this new AI-developed vaccine help prevent the next pandemic?

media:group.media:title: Can this new AI-developed vaccine help prevent the next pandemic?
media:group.media:description:
What if vaccines could stay effective even as viruses mutate? 💉
Researchers at Cambridge have used AI to develop a bird flu vaccine that gave animals complete protection against multiple variants in a new study.
The next step? Human clinical trials.
Find out more 👉 https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/AI-developed-vaccines-against-viruses

entry.title: Can this new AI-developed vaccine help prevent the next pandemic?

media:group.media:title: Can this new AI-developed vaccine help prevent the next pandemic?
media:group.media:description:
Cambridge scientists use AI to develop bird flu vaccine that outperforms current stockpiled jab
Bird flu is spreading in animals around the world and is considered a significant threat to human health. Although some human infections with the North American variants have been mild, other variants in south-east Asia have caused severe disease and high mortality in humans.
A Cambridge team led by Professor Jonathan Heeney has used AI to engineer a new candidate bird flu vaccine that outperforms the jabs currently stockpiled by governments around the world, in case of a human outbreak.
A new successful trial provides further evidence that the team’s ‘plug and play’ approach could be used to create safe, highly effective vaccines for a plethora of infectious diseases threatening human health globally, including Ebola and Marburg viruses, amongst some of the most dangerous human pathogens in the world.
This new class of vaccines not only protect against many variants simultaneously, but may also provide protection against related viruses that have not yet emerged or spilled over into humans.
The technology could be a game changer for pandemic preparedness, health security and national biosecurity.
Find out more here 👉 https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/AI-developed-vaccines-against-viruses

entry.title: Physicists knock at the door of the zeptoverse

media:group.media:title: Physicists knock at the door of the zeptoverse
media:group.media:description:
Have you ever heard of a zeptometre? It's a trillionth of a billionth of a metre, billions of times smaller than a single atom.
A Cambridge-led team of physicists, working at CERN, have detected an ultra-rare decay of a subatomic particle called a beauty quark, a process which occurs in just one in ten billion beauty quarks.
The way these tiny particles decay could help us understand what new physics might exist at the zeptometre scale.
This strange world, dubbed the zeptoverse, could also be hiding the secrets of dark matter, or help us understand how matter came into being during the Big Bang.
Find out more: https://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/physicists-knock-at-the-door-of-the-zeptoverse?utm_campaign=research&utm_medium=social&utm_source=youtube

media:group.media:title: Algae: Nature's Tiny Power Plant
media:group.media:description:
Cambridge researchers have created a device that could replace millions of small disposable batteries with a much cleaner source of energy.
A team at the Department of Biochemistry has found a way to tap into the natural process of photosynthesis in algae and use it to generate continuous electricity 24/7 – without harming the organism at all.
Because it's powered by a living organism, this 'biocell' technology can keep producing electricity for as long as the algae remains alive. The record so far? Six years and counting...
This represents a completely new way to generate electricity that can continue operating, even when there's no light at all.
The team is now in talks with potential clients through its spin-out company and is excited about the technology's wide range of applications.
Find out more: https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/cambridge-algae-power-to-replace-batteries
#CambridgeUniversity #CambridgeResearch #Cambridge #Biocells

entry.title: You'll Fit In 2026 at Trinity Hall

media:group.media:title: You'll Fit In 2026 at Trinity Hall
media:group.media:description:
Are you a Year 12 UK student and thinking about applying to Cambridge? 💭
If you're from an underrepresented group, this opportunity might be for you.
Trinity Hall's 'You'll Fit In' programme aims to support students from backgrounds that are underrepresented at Cambridge.
It will cover all aspects of the admissions process, and aims to give potential applicants a chance to experience what life as a Cambridge student could be like.
Apply before the 8 December deadline through this link: https://www.trinhall.cam.ac.uk/study-with-us/access-and-outreach/widening-participation/youll-fit-in/
